power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Evaluating the mobile MUSE EEG headband for studying resting state EEG and event-related potentials

author.affiliation:
School of Business, Social and Decision Sciences
								Constructor University
								
									Bremen
									Germany

text.text: Objectives: We examined whether and how tactile EEG experiments could be done through self-assessments by participants at home or through online experiments with consumer-grade mobile EEG devices.
As a first step towards this aim, we performed a Flanker task in an online scenario with a MUSE headband and similarly a conventional lab experiment with a standard EEG device.

Methods: Five undergraduate students participated in a visual flanker experiment and associated ERP components were recorded with either a standard 32-channel EEG System or a 4-channel MUSE EEG headband.
In addition, we performed a 2-minutes resting state recording.
Results: Resting state brain oscillations measured with the Muse device revealed a similar pattern as with a standard EEG machine, however, strength of alpha oscillations was significantly reduced.
For the Flanker task, in the Muse data, the stimulus-locked ERP components were less visible as compared to standard EEG, still the N200 was clearly expressed for the correct trials.
Interestingly, in the incorrect trials, time-locked to the response there was the same negative Ne component visible as for the standard experiment.
Conclusion: Our results reveal that the Muse device is suitable to obtain event-related potentials -even from interpolated electrode channels.
Advanced preprocessing and artifact removal algorithms specifically targeting such devices with only a few and peripheral channels might help to better isolate ERP components of interest.
It remains the challenge to develop devices and procedures for online tactile testing.
We examined whether and how tactile EEG experiments could be done through selfassessments by participants at home or through online experiments with consumer-grade mobile EEG devices.

Such devices are available at low costs of a few hundred Euros and companies selling these devices claim that they are able to measure brain oscillations and can be used to learn to entrain such oscillations, for example, for relaxation or facilitation of attention.
One example of such devices is the Muse EEG headband (InteraXon, Ontario, Canada).
text.formatted: One example of such devices is the Muse EEG headband <ref type="bibr">(InteraXon, Ontario, Canada)</ref>.

text.text: It is easy to use and based on detailed instructions users can setup the device by themselves for measuring EEG data.
The MUSE EEG system has four electrodes located analogous to Fpz, AF7, AF8, TP9, and TP10 with electrode Fpz utilized as the reference electrode.
Raw data are recorded with a sampling rate of 256 Hz and can be streamed to other devices via Bluetooth for recording, storage, and analysis.

It has been shown previously that the Muse device not only offers the opportunity to measure and record ongoing brain oscillations but that it is in principle able to also reveal standard ERP components such as the N200 or P300 in visual oddball or the response positivity in reward-learning experiments (Krigolson et al., 2017).
text.formatted: It has been shown previously that the Muse device not only offers the opportunity to measure and record ongoing brain oscillations but that it is in principle able to also reveal standard ERP components such as the N200 or P300 in visual oddball or the response positivity in reward-learning experiments <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Krigolson et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Critical issues with using such devices for scientific experiments is the given layout of the electrodes not covering standard frontal, central, or parietal electrode locations and the need to synchronize the recording with behavioral data.

While the latter can be achieved by recording and synchronizing both type of data by one master computer (as being standard in EEG studies) the former requires extrapolation of additional electrode channels through the data from the 4 existing electrodes.
Further, when doing online or selfadministered experiments, storage of and access to the data by the experimenter needs to be possible.
Also, easy and comprehensive instructions for the participants are required.
Finally, when doing tactile experiments, the hardest problem is to provide mobile tactile stimulation devices to the participants.

In our experiment we aimed at doing the first steps towards such studies, i.e., doing an online cognitive experiment and online EEG data collection with the Muse device and evaluate the results against recordings with a standard EEG system in our lab.
As cognitive paradigm we chose a standard Flanker task where we expected to reveal the well-known error-related negativity (ERN or Ne; Falkenstein et al., 2000).
text.formatted: As cognitive paradigm we chose a standard Flanker task where we expected to reveal the well-known error-related negativity (ERN or Ne; <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Falkenstein et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: As the Ne is most pronounced at frontocentral electrodes, this paradigm would also allow us to examine whether interpolation of activity at such locations by the activity of the recorded electrodes would be possible and reveal reliable results.
To test the principal usability of the device for EEG recordings we also applied a standard resting state EEG paradigm with eyes closed.
The Muse experiment was performed as online experiment in one joint session within the classroom, however, each participant worked independently with own mobile computers connected to the internet.
Instead of the response pads as used in the standard EEG experiment, the computer keyboard was used in the Flanker task.
Each participant was provided with their own Muse headbands and detailed instructions on how to use the device, how to conduct the experiment, and how to store the data.
This arrangement allowed close supervision of how the experiments were done and if all instructions given beforehand were sufficient so that the participants could do the experiments on their own.
This was always the case and there was no need for the experimenter to interfere.
EEG data in the MUSE session were recorded from the MUSE EEG headband with 256 Hz sampling rate.
Data from the MUSE EEG system were streamed via Bluetooth to the Muse EEG Explorer software running in a web browser (https://muse-eeg-app.web.app/; Castillo & Shaked, 2017).
text.formatted: Data from the MUSE EEG system were streamed via Bluetooth to the Muse EEG Explorer software running in a web browser (<ref type="url" target="https://muse-eeg-app.web.app/">https://muse-eeg-app.web.app/</ref>; <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Castillo & Shaked, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: After recording, all EEG data were automatically downloaded to the local PC as CSV file with corresponding time information in universal Unix time format.
The Flanker experiment was programmed and conducted similarly to the standard experiment on the Psytoolkit online platform (https://www.psytoolkit.org/; Stoet, 2017 Stoet, , 2020)).
text.formatted: The Flanker experiment was programmed and conducted similarly to the standard experiment on the Psytoolkit online platform (<ref type="url" target="https://www.psytoolkit.org/">https://www.psytoolkit.org/</ref>; <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Stoet, 2017</ref> <ref type="bibr">Stoet, , 2020))</ref>.

text.text: Event files from the Flanker experiment were stored locally as CSV files and contained time information of all stimulus and response events as described above.
Again, time information was stored in Unix format so that both files, the EEG data file and the Flanker data file could be exactly synchronized.
For standard analysis of the EEG data obtained with the Biosemi system, data were processed offline with EEGLAB under MATLAB.
For resting state data analysis, from the ongoing EEG a 2-minute period was extracted.
Data were re-referenced to an average mastoid and then filtered using a bandpass filter with a passband of 1 Hz to 30 Hz in addition to a 50 Hz notch filter.
Data from all 5 participants was merged and EEG power spectral density was plotted over the frequency range of 2-25 Hz with the spectopo function in EEGLAB.
For comparison with the Muse data, only resting state data for electrodes AF7, AF8, TP9, and TP10 are presented below.
For the Flanker task, the bandpass filter was set to 0.1 to 30 Hz.
Mean response times were between 350 and 400 ms and the Ne is expected around 100 ms after the response.
Thus, segments encompassing the onset of each response (from 500 ms before to 200 ms after) were extracted from the continuous EEG.
Following segmentation, independent component analysis was used to correct ocular and muscle artifacts.
Following this, all segments were baseline corrected using a time window from -500 to -450 ms preceding the stimulus onset.
For each participant and separately for correct and incorrect reposnes, ERP waveforms were created by averaging the segmented EEG data for each electrode.
Again, segments of all 5 participants then were merged into one single dataset.
For MUSE EEG data, electrode Fz was interpolated from the other 4 electrodes because we expected the error-related negativity (Ne) to be represented at that electrode.

Further filtering, segmentation, and merging of the datasets was done identically to the standard EEG analysis except the artifact removal through ICA decomposition as no separate ocular recordings were available.
Resting state data and associated spectrograms for both the Biosemi and the Muse data are shown in figure 2.
text.formatted: Resting state data and associated spectrograms for both the Biosemi and the Muse data are shown in figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>.

text.text: Note: electrodes Fp1, Fp2, T7, and T8 in the Biosemi data correspond with the electrodes AF7, AF8, TP9, and TP10, respectively, in the Muse data.
The Biosemi data reveal the expected strong alpha peak at around 9-11 Hz.
For the Muse data, the alpha peak is also visible but severely reduced.

Whether the reduced alpha peak amplitude in the Muse experiment results from differences in the scenario (classroom versus quiet room) or from more noise in the Muse data remains open and requires further assessments.

Nevertheless, our results reveal that brain oscillations can be measured with the Muse device and that it might be possible to generate meaningful data even in unsupervised or online experiments.  a positive deflection about 100 ms after stimulus onset (P100) and a negative deflection about 200 ms after stimulus onset (N200).
Further, a P200 and P300 can be identified.
For the incorrect trials, these later componentsP200 and P300 are replaced by a negative deflection about 50-100 ms after the response -presumably the Ne -followed by another positive component.
In the Muse data, the stimulus-locked ERP components are less impressed, still the N200 is clearly visible for the correct trials.
Interestingly, in the incorrect trials, time-locked to the response there is again the same negative Ne component visible as for the standard experiment.
Our results herewith reveal that the Muse devices are suitable to obtain event-related potentials -even from interpolated electrode channels.
Advanced preprocessing and artifact removal algorithms specifically targeting such devices with only a few and peripheral channels might help to better isolate ERP components of interest.
The actual versions of the Muse also allow the connection of a 5th electrode via an auxiliary USB connector.
This would enable researchers to place an additional electrode anywhere on the scalp, for measuring ERPs without the need for interpolation.
For tactile experiments done through self-assessment or even online still the problem of tactile stimulation needs to be solved and respective devices to be developed.

text.text: undergraduate students from a neuroscience methods course at Constructor University participated in the experiment.

Participants performed the same two experimental tasks (Flanker task and resting state EEG) in two separate sessions while collecting their EEG data with either the Muse portable EEG headband or a Biosemi EEG System with a standard 10-20 electrode configuration and a typical EEG set-up (stimulus machine, recording machine, etc.).
For collecting standard EEG data, a 32-channel active electrode system (ActiveTwo, BioSemi, Amsterdam, Netherlands) was used with electrodes placed according to the 10-20 system.

Additionally, the active Common Mode Sense (CMS) electrode and the passive Driven Right Leg (DRL) electrode were affixed next to Cz and used as reference and ground electrodes, respectively (cf. http://www.biosemi/faq/cms&drl.htm).
text.formatted: Additionally, the active Common Mode Sense (CMS) electrode and the passive Driven Right Leg (DRL) electrode were affixed next to Cz and used as reference and ground electrodes, respectively (cf. http://www.biosemi/faq/cms&drl.htm).

text.text: Vertical and horizontal eye movements as well as mastoid potentials were recorded with six facial electrodes designed for bodysurface applications.
The signal was digitized with a sampling rate of 2048 Hz and online bandpass filtered between 0.16 and 100 Hz.
Participants were seated in front of a 19″ LCD computer monitor in a quiet and closed room as usual.
For recording 2 minutes of resting state EEG data participants were told to close their eyes and to relax.
Participants then completed 400 trials of a Flanker task with 4 conditions (100 trials each).

The flanker paradigm consisted of arrowheads pointing to the left or right which were flanked by 2 other arrowheads on both sides pointing to the same (congruent condition: >>>>> or <<<<<) or opposite direction (incongruent condition: >><>> or <<><<).
